items.title: Michael White interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 10, 2025
items.q: You know near the end I sat in with him a couple of times, like in Chicago at the Chicago Jazz Fest.

ctx.x: Yes. And he kind of found that out near the end. But for most of my life I didn’t like it. People thought I couldn’t get into that and this, that and the other. But I met a clarinet player, Perry Robinson, who was from New York and he was an underground legend of the loft movement of the ‘60s and he played and recorded with a number of people in the avant garde vein. He was an older guy, and he came down to New Orleans to play. And, long story short, I sat in with him and he kept asking me to sit in. There were…

to get back to some state of normalcy, or living in the new existence. It was very painful. There were a lot of losses. I went through a plethora of emotions: bewilderment, anger, you know of being frightened, fear. Little joy here and there. And I needed to express those things. I wrote a bunch of songs at a artist’s retreat here called Studio in the Woods, A Studio in the Woods. And I recorded them on a recording called “Blue Crescent.” And the idea was it was kind of like my version of the state of New Orleans…

especially to things that have rhythm. I realized in the old days the train was a very important part of, you know early blues and jazz, the rhythm of the train and the symbolism of the train. It represented progress, it represented movement, it represented freedom, it represented going north and all of those things. But at the same time it gave great rhythms that you could, you know, take off on on songs. So now I try to hear rhythm through things. And It’s simple things now that catch my attention. It might be…
